new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (PDF 1.4, 4 pp, text, the PDF's metadata gives the title 'OPD', author 'SIL PNG Branch', printed 2004-09-07). extracted text shows, on physical page 3 (footer 'Tauade OPD Printed: September 7, 2004 Page 3'), the heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' followed by exactly: 'Stress always seems to occur on the first heavy syllable of the word. Words with syllables of equal weight usually have stress on the first syllable.' Quote matches the report verbatim (single line-break at 'weight / usually' in the PDF). Immediately below is the 'Syllable Patterns' table listing V, VC, VV, CV, CVC, CVV, CVVC with examples (ip 'water', au 'but', val 'back', mii 'shoot', kaut 'lime', pu.lai…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the leftmost heavy syllable of the word; if all syllables are of equal weight (no heavy syllable, or all equally heavy), stress defaults to the initial syllable. The OPD's syllable-pattern table (p. 3) lists VC, VV, CVC, CVV, CVVC alongside V and CV, so 'heavy' presumably means closed or long-vowel/diphthong syllables; the OPD does not define weight explicitly.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the statement is hedged ('always seems to', 'usually').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('of the word'); a 4-page SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (draft, no peer review), based on the Stutzmans' fieldwork (data checked March 1992). No tone or length contrast is claimed in the suprasegmental section, though vowel sequences/long vowels (ii, ee, aa, oo, uu) appear in the inventory.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Tauade [ttd] of Central Province (major village Sopu), labelled 'Goilalan Family' in the SIL sheet; Glottolog 5.1 treats taua1242 as an isolate. No dialect is specified. Alternate names in the record: Tauata, Afoa, Goilala, Ambo(-Deba).

tone_statements.citation: Dutton, Tom E. 1975. South-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum Languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study Vol. 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 613-664. Canberra: ANU.
tone_statements.quote: Vowel systems are simple and based on five vowels (i, e, a, o, u). Some languages are tonal but stress is generally important and related to intonation which may be quite complex. Many languages also have complex morphophonemic rules.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.note: p. 3, 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': stress always seems to fall on the first heavy syllable of the word; words whose syllables are of equal weight usually stress the first syllable. Syllable-pattern table on the same page (V, VC, VV, CV, CVC, CVV, CVVC) shows closed and long-vowel/diphthong syllables, i.e. the heavy types.

No descriptive (grammar/phonology/sketch) references listed; only overviews (Dutton 1975, Ray 1929, Ray 1913-14) and wordlists (Egidi 1907, Strong 1912, Anonymous 1914, Humphries 1922, Fastre 1920). Nothing on stress.
Stub; no phonology section; notes PARADISEC TD1 (Dutton) holds Tauade materials.

sources.note: Only tone remark: tone modification is not among the morphological processes found in Tauade word formation (inflection is by suffixation only); says nothing on whether the language has lexical tone.

tone.quote: Tauade is an agglutinative or concatenative language. Inflection is done by suffixation only. None of the other morphological processes, such as infixation, reduplication, vowel change, tone modification, discontinuous morphemes, phonological feature modification, stress modification, or subtraction have been discovered so far in Tauade word formation.

tone.says: No Tauade-specific tone or stress statement anywhere (the Tauade section, p. 632, is about location, lexicostatistics and mission literacy materials only).
